standard.title: Develop criteria collaboratively
standard.description: develop design criteria collaboratively including sustainability to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can negotiate design criteria, including sustainability, to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions (AC9TDE6P04). They have used given or negotiated criteria but have not yet developed criteria collaboratively from scratch, incorporated Safety by Design principles, or used evaluation to drive iterative modification of processes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop design criteria collaboratively — covering accessibility, aesthetics, functionality, sustainability and Safety by Design principles — and use these criteria to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions, iterating and modifying based on evaluation.

nodes.label: What makes good design criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what design criteria are and why they need to cover multiple dimensions including sustainability
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three dimensions that design criteria should address (e.g. accessibility, aesthetics, functionality, sustainability); explain why evaluating against criteria is more useful than evaluating by personal preference
nodes.typical_width: Explain how criteria across different dimensions can complement or conflict; identify Safety by Design principles (prevention, protection, proactive change) as a specific criteria framework
wider: Apply life cycle assessment as a criteria framework — how does evaluating across the full product lifecycle change what criteria are prioritised?
Limited width — understanding what criteria are is a single conceptual insight. The breadth comes from applying criteria to different design challenges at later nodes.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who develop vague or single-dimension criteria at Node 2 will produce evaluations at Nodes 3–5 that miss trade-offs between dimensions — the multi-dimensional criteria framework must be understood before it can be applied collaboratively or used to drive iteration.
success_criteria: Identifies at least three dimensions that design criteria should address
Explains why criteria-based evaluation is more useful than personal preference

response_modes.reason: Students who develop vague criteria ('make it good') or single-dimension criteria ('make it sustainable') will produce evaluations that miss important trade-offs. Understanding that criteria must be specific, multi-dimensional and assessable is the foundation for useful evaluation at Nodes 2 and 3.

nodes.label: Developing criteria collaboratively
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop design criteria through collaboration, incorporating input from multiple perspectives including potential users
nodes.minimum_width: Develop at least three design criteria collaboratively with peers; ensure at least one addresses sustainability
nodes.typical_width: Develop criteria collaboratively by recording goals from prospective users, incorporating accessibility and Safety by Design principles, and ensuring criteria are specific enough to evaluate against
wider: Develop criteria through consultation with community members from diverse backgrounds, including those who communicate in languages other than English
Compare criteria developed by different groups for the same design challenge — how does who participates change what gets prioritised?
nodes.hinge_reason: The collaboratively developed criteria from this node are the evaluation instrument for Nodes 3, 4 and 5 — without specific, multi-dimensional criteria in hand, students cannot apply them to existing products, drive iterative design decisions, or conduct meaningful final evaluation.
success_criteria: Develops at least three criteria collaboratively
At least one criterion addresses sustainability
Criteria are specific enough to evaluate a design against

response_modes.reason: Developing criteria collaboratively surfaces different perspectives only when students encounter diverse stakeholders and communities. A group of similar students will develop similar criteria. Seeing how criteria change when different community members participate — including those from diverse backgrounds or who communicate in languages other than English — builds understanding that criteria are not neutral.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The community consultation and cross-group comparison directions offer advancing students genuinely rich insight into how collaborative processes shape outcomes — comparing criteria from different groups for the same challenge reveals how participant diversity affects what gets prioritised.

nodes.label: Applying criteria to analyse existing products
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply collaboratively developed criteria to evaluate existing designed solutions and extract insights that inform their own design brief.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate at least one existing product against two collaboratively developed criteria; identify at least one design insight that will inform your own solution.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate multiple existing products against all developed criteria; compare what works and what doesn't; document insights as design constraints or opportunities for your own solution.
wider: Compare existing products from different cultural or geographic contexts against the same criteria — how does context change what 'good design' means?
Evaluate products at different price or quality tiers and explain how criteria satisfaction varies.
success_criteria: Evaluates at least one existing product against collaboratively developed criteria
Identifies at least one design insight that will inform their own solution

response_modes.reason: Applying criteria to existing products requires students to reason from evidence: criterion → what does the product do → does it satisfy the criterion → what does this tell us about our own design. Students who describe products without applying criteria produce observations rather than insights.

nodes.label: Evaluating and iterating during design
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate design ideas and processes against criteria during the design cycle and iterate based on that evaluation.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate a design against at least two criteria during the design process; identify at least one improvement and modify the design accordingly.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate and iterate across the design process — not just the final product; re-evaluate after modification to confirm improvement; document what changed and why.
wider: Transfer evaluation skills from one design challenge to another — what criteria and lessons carry across contexts?
Limited width — iterative evaluation is a consistent process. The breadth comes from the variety of design challenges.
success_criteria: Evaluates a design against at least two criteria during the design process
Modifies the design based on the evaluation and explains the change

response_modes.reason: Evaluating and iterating during design requires applying collaboratively developed criteria (node 2) to live design decisions. Students who treat evaluation as a final step rather than a design tool produce designs that don't improve through the process.

nodes.label: Final evaluation against criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate a completed designed solution against all collaboratively developed criteria and articulate what they would change in a future iteration.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate the completed solution against at least two collaboratively developed criteria; identify at least one thing that would be done differently.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the completed solution across all criteria dimensions; reflect on how the design process shaped the outcome; identify improvements for a future iteration and explain why.
wider: Evaluate how iterative modification throughout the project improved the final outcome compared to what an initial design would have produced.
Assess how well the collaboratively developed criteria captured what actually mattered — would you develop different criteria next time?
success_criteria: Evaluates the completed solution against all collaboratively developed criteria
Identifies at least one specific improvement for a future iteration

response_modes.reason: Final evaluation requires students to reason from evidence across the whole project: what did the criteria require → what did the solution achieve → where did it fall short → what would change. Students who produce vague reflections have not applied criteria rigorously.
